tfn.why: The text says: "It started in 2011 and is run by a company called Client Partners."

tfn.s: The service is the largest of its kind in Japan.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say how big the service is compared with others.

tfn.s: Every worker in the service is a real grandmother.
tfn.why: The text says the opposite: "Not every worker is actually a grandmother, and the service is not only for people who feel lonely."

tfn.s: Taeko Kaji was 69 when she spoke to journalists in 2025.
tfn.why: The text says: "One woman working for the service, Taeko Kaji, was 69 when she spoke to Australian journalists in 2025."

tfn.s: It is easy for families who live far away to drop in for an hour.

focus.note: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word such as up or out. The small word changes the meaning, so learn the two words together.

tfn.s: The writer implies that customers should not expect a hired visitor to become a relative.
tfn.why: The text says the relationship is "explicitly professional" and that neither motive "makes the visitor a relative".

tfn.s: The writer argues that the service will push families to take on more responsibility for older relatives.
tfn.why: The text warns that a commercial solution "quietly relieves families" of obligations.

tfn.s: Most of the women who work for the service used to have jobs in caring.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text says nothing about the women's earlier careers.

tfn.s: Taeko Kaji's experience supports the view that older people can be skilled contributors.
tfn.why: The text says her positive account "challenges a persistent assumption" that older people are mainly recipients of care.

tfn.s: The writer regards paying for support outside the family as a modern invention.
tfn.why: The text says people "have always sought wisdom and support beyond their immediate families"; only the honesty of the financial terms may be new.

speak.title: Role-play: should we hire a grandmother?
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: Your father lives alone and you live far away. You want to book a paid visitor from a service like OK! Obaachan for two hours a week. Explain why it could help, listen to his worries and try to agree a plan.

b.text: You're proud and independent. You think paid company is strange, and you'd rather see your family. Say what worries you. You can say no, or agree to try it if the conditions are right.

phrases: I'm worried you're on your own too much.
It's only a trial, so we could try it once.
I don't want a stranger in my house.
She'd help with the cooking, and she'd be good company.
I'd rather see you than pay someone.
Let's try it for a month and see how it goes.
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: did the father agree, and what changed his mind?
